options.text: Each triangle has an angle sum of $180^{\circ}$, and the six triangle angles together make the four angles of $ABCD$, so the sum is $2\times180^{\circ}=360^{\circ}$.
Each triangle has an angle sum of $180^{\circ}$, but the two triangles share the diagonal, so the sum is $2\times180^{\circ}-180^{\circ}=180^{\circ}$.
options.why: The shared diagonal is a side, not an angle, so nothing is counted twice and nothing should be subtracted.

options.text: The diagonal meets the sides at right angles, creating four right angles, and $4\times90^{\circ}=360^{\circ}$.
options.why: A diagonal does not meet the sides at right angles, and it creates two angles at each end, not four right angles.

options.text: A quadrilateral has four sides and each side contributes $90^{\circ}$, giving $4\times90^{\circ}=360^{\circ}$.
options.why: Sides do not carry an angle measure, and this reasoning would wrongly force every quadrilateral to have four right angles.

questions.solution_text:
In $\triangle ABD$: $\angle DAB+\angle ABD+\angle ADB=180^{\circ}$, angle sum of a triangle
In $\triangle BCD$: $\angle BCD+\angle DBC+\angle BDC=180^{\circ}$, angle sum of a triangle
The two angles at $B$ join to make $\angle ABC$ and the two at $D$ join to make $\angle ADC$, so the four angles of $ABCD$ total $180^{\circ}+180^{\circ}=360^{\circ}$.
